summary.title: Deep Lessons from Google and eBay on Building Ecosystems of Microservices
summary.one_liner: Learn how large systems at Google and eBay evolve into ecosystems of polyglot microservices, and how aligned incentives, chargebacks, and service ownership keep them healthy.
keywords: how do standards evolve without architects
how to scale an engineering organization
takeaways: Large-scale systems at Google, eBay, Twitter and Amazon tend to evolve from monoliths into graphs of polyglot microservices, mostly through evolution rather than top-down design.
Charging internal customers for services and defining SLAs aligns incentives so both sides use resources efficiently and keep quality high.
Each service should be single-purpose, own its persistence, and be owned end-to-end by a small team ('you build it, you run it').
Standardize the communication arcs and common infrastructure rather than service internals; encourage best practices with libraries, code review and code search instead of central review boards.
Operate with predictable tail latency, incremental canary rollouts, feature flags, and avoid mega-services and shared databases.
summary.summary: This High Scalability article summarizes a talk by Randy Shoup, who worked at Google and eBay, on service architectures at scale. It walks through how systems at Google, eBay, Twitter and Amazon evolved into polyglot microservices and how ecosystems of services grow bottom-up. It then covers building a service (ownership, chargebacks, compatibility), operating at scale (tail latency, canaries, feature flags), and anti-patterns such as mega-services and shared persistence. The page is organized as a bulleted outline of the talk's sections.
